rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse challenges idolaters to substantiate their claim that idols participate in creation; it invokes questions showing that no one created the heavens or earth besides God.
rows.anchor: challenges the idolaters to substantiate their claim that their idols have some part in the creative process

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the phrase manifest error, the commentary directs readers to its discussion at 36:24.
rows.anchor: For manifest error , see 36:24c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the smallest good or evil deed will be brought forth and accounted for on the Day of Judgment, as 99:7–8 teaches.
rows.anchor: All deeds, no matter how small, will be accounted for on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's mustard-seed image also indicates that all deeds will be weighed on the Day of Resurrection, with no soul wronged.
rows.anchor: Thus it is said that all deeds will be weighed, as in 21:47

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Subtle because He knows the minutest details, and Aware because He knows all things at every moment.
rows.anchor: Subtle indicates that God has knowledge of the minutest details, while Aware indicates that He is aware of all things at every moment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh idolaters acknowledged God as creator because a supreme creator was evident to them and many still believed in a supreme deity.
rows.anchor: the idolaters among the Quraysh—would surely say, “God” (cf. 10:31

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Praise for the created order belongs to God alone, not to beings that did not create it.
rows.anchor: only God should be praised for the existence of the created order, not those who had nothing to do with bringing forth creation (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: The command to praise God means that no being other than God should be worshipped.
rows.anchor: no being other than God should be worshipped (Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the Divine Names the Self-Sufficient and the Praised, the commentary refers to its note on 31:12.
rows.anchor: Regarding the Divine Names the Self-Sufficient, the Praised, see 31:12c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image conveys the inexhaustibility of God's creative speech, as in the command Be, through which creation comes into being.
rows.anchor: This verse evokes the inexhaustibility of God’s creation through Divine Speech

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this context, seven more seas is figurative language for an immeasurable quantity, not a literal count.
rows.anchor: seven more is not literal, but is meant to indicate an immeasurable quantity (IK, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God's possible creations are infinite, even innumerable pens and immeasurable seas of ink would be exhausted before His creative speech.
rows.anchor: immeasurable seas of ink and innumerable pens would be exhausted before God’s creative speech would be exhausted

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One account says the verse followed a dispute in Madinah: Jewish leaders asked whether the little knowledge mentioned in 17:85 meant theirs or the Muslims'; Muhammad answered both, and said God's knowledge dwarfed theirs despite the Torah's clarification.
rows.anchor: Then God sent this verse in response to what they had asked (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: W
rows.claim: Another account has the Prophet say their knowledge was little beside God's, though sufficient if practiced; Jews raised the apparent tension with wisdom as much good, and the verse was revealed in reply.
rows.anchor: Then as a response, God revealed this verse (W)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Others say the verse may have answered disbelievers who claimed that Muhammad's revelations would soon be exhausted.
rows.anchor: Others say that this verse may have been revealed in relation to a group of disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic angelology identifies the Angel of Death as Azrael, who removes spirits from bodies at death.
rows.anchor: the Angel of death is understood to be Azrael (IK, Q), who is in charge of removing spirits from bodies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Angel of Death is said to have angelic helpers in taking souls, while another verse says God takes souls at death.
rows.anchor: he is said to have helpers among the angels (IK, Ṭ; see 4:97c; 8:50; 16:32), though it is also said that God takes souls

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī reconciles the accounts: the Angel of Death seizes souls, helping angels attend them, and God brings about their end.
rows.anchor: Al-Qurṭubī reconciles these verses by saying that the Angel of Death seizes them

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: One reading takes the address “Couldst thou but see” as directed specifically to the Prophet; either way it expresses amazement at the disbelievers' Hereafter state.
rows.anchor: Couldst thou but see is an address directly to the Prophet

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another reading takes the address as general rather than directed specifically to the Prophet; either way it conveys amazement at the disbelievers' Hereafter state.
rows.anchor: a general address (R). In either case, it refers to the amazement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guilty have died, witnessed the Resurrection and Judgment they denied, and admitted their sin.
rows.anchor: seen the realities of Resurrection and Judgment that they had denied

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: “We are certain” may mean that they now believe with certainty.
rows.anchor: We are certain, meaning they believe with certainty

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Alternatively, they may merely claim belief to try to escape punishment, as in their denial of idolatry elsewhere.
rows.anchor: simply claiming to believe in order to avoid the punishment, as in 6:23

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God refuses return requests: 35:37 answers with the time and warning already given, 23:100 calls the request mere words, and 6:28 says returnees would repeat their forbidden conduct.
rows.anchor: God thus denies all such requests, because even if they were sent back, they would return to the very thing they had been forbidden

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: The lesser punishment is punishment in this worldly life.
rows.anchor: The lesser punishment is punishment in this world (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Worldly punishment can take the form of defeat and humiliation, illness, natural disaster, or other afflictions.
rows.anchor: through the humiliation of defeat, through illness, or by natural disaster (JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Others identify the lesser punishment as legal penalties against disbelievers in this world or punishment in the grave before the eternal punishment.
rows.anchor: Others say it refers to the legal punishments brought against the disbelievers in this world or to the punishment in the grave

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The greater punishment is the punishment of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The greater punishment is that of the Hereafter (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The lesser affliction can be a mercy if it prompts reflection and return to belief, the human being's natural state.
rows.anchor: they are afflicted with the lesser punishment as a mercy from God, as it might make them reflect and thus turn back to belief

rows.speaker: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says Muslims formerly called Zayd ibn Ḥārithah “Zayd ibn Muhammad” until this revelation instructed them to name adopted children after their fathers.
rows.anchor: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar is reported to have said, “We did not use to call Zayd ibn Ḥārithah by any name other than Zayd ibn Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse ends the pre-Islamic practice of adopting others as the Prophet adopted Zayd and directs Muslims to relate instead as brothers and clients.
rows.anchor: This verse abolished the pre-Islamic custom of adopting others the way the Prophet had adopted Zayd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clients” translates mawālī, plural of mawlā, a term used for heirs, God as Master, and varied close relationships; mawlā is etymologically related to walī, protector or protecting friend.
rows.anchor: Clients translates mawālī (sing. mawlā), which is elsewhere translated heirs

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Those who practiced adoption as the Prophet did with Zayd are not blamed because they did not intend to oppose God's will.
rows.anchor: There is no blame upon those who had engaged in the practice of adoption as the Prophet did in Zayd’s case

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More broadly, people are not held accountable for unintended mistakes.
rows.anchor: Applied more broadly, this verse is understood to mean that people are not taken to account for unintended mistakes

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that God exempts his community from mistakes, forgetfulness, and acts done under compulsion.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said, “God exonerates my community of being mistaken, of forgetting, and of that which they are forced to do”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This often cited verse is central to understanding the Prophet's place in Islam.
rows.anchor: This frequently cited verse is among the most important in the Quran for understanding the place of the Prophet in Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In its immediate context, the verse explains why the Prophet should be obeyed, is a beautiful example and a luminous lamp, and has distinctive marital and family rulings.
rows.anchor: it answers questions one might ask of the previous verses: why the Prophet should be obeyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Invoke blessings translates ṣallā/yuṣallī, from the same root as ṣalāh, prayer.
rows.anchor: Invoke blessings translates the verb ṣallā/yuṣallī, which is from the same rootas ṣalāh

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Commentators distinguish the senses: God's ṣalāh is loving Mercy, while the angels' ṣalāh is seeking forgiveness.
rows.anchor: God’s ṣalāh is loving Mercy and that of the angels is seeking forgiveness (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Human beings invoke blessings by supplicating for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Human beings then invoke blessings by supplicating for the Prophet (Aj)

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Human beings also invoke blessings by following and loving the Prophet.
rows.anchor: by following him and loving him (Su)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When Companions asked how to bless him after learning the greeting of peace, the Prophet taught a supplication asking God to bless and shower grace on Muhammad and his family as on Abraham and his family.
rows.anchor: To which he answered,“O God! Bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad as Thou hast blessed Abraham

rows.speaker: al-Ālūsī
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says asking God to bless the Prophet acknowledges that people can do no more than request God's blessings.
rows.anchor: the manner in which human beings invoke blessings upon the Prophet, by calling for God’s Blessings upon him, means that they are in fact realizing their inability

rows.speaker: K
rows.claim: Metaphysically, only God invokes blessings upon the Prophet; human prayer participates in and affirms the Divine Act.
rows.anchor: in all modes of asking blessing upon the Prophet, it is only God Who invokes blessings upon him (K)

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet reports Gabriel's message that God blesses tenfold anyone in the community who blesses the Prophet and returns peace tenfold to anyone who greets him.
rows.anchor: No member of thy community invokes blessings upon thee but that I bless him tenfold

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet calls a person miserly if his name is mentioned in that person's presence and the person does not bless him.
rows.anchor: The miser is one who when I am mentioned in his presence does not invoke blessings upon me

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When a man supplicated hastily, the Prophet instructed him to praise God first, bless the Prophet next, and then supplicate as he wished.
rows.anchor: When one makes supplication, let him begin by praising God. Then let him invoke blessings upon the Prophet.

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: ʿUmar says a supplication remains suspended between Heaven and earth until blessings are invoked upon the Prophet.
rows.anchor: A supplication is suspended between Heaven and earth and does not ascend any further until you invoke blessings upon your Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Blessing the Prophet benefits believers rather than the Prophet, so the verse is understood as a command to all believers.
rows.anchor: invoking blessings upon the Prophet is not a benefit for the Prophet, but for the believers themselves

rows.speaker: IK, Q, R
rows.claim: Some consider blessing the Prophet commendable, while others consider it obligatory.
rows.anchor: Some say that invoking blessings upon the Prophet is a commendable deed

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Among those who regard it as obligatory, some require blessings once in a lifetime, while others require them in every prayer.
rows.anchor: Some maintain that its being obligatory may simply mean that such blessings must be invoked at some point during the course of one’s life

rows.speaker: Imam al-Shāfiʿī and many followers of his legal tradition
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī and many followers hold that a prayer is valid only if blessings are invoked upon the Prophet in every prayer.
rows.anchor: According to Imam al-Shāfiʿī and many followers of his legal tradition, one must invoke blessings upon the Prophet in every prayer

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Blessing the Prophet draws one nearer to God: increased invocation engenders love for the Prophet, then love for God, whose love draws the person to His Presence.
rows.anchor: invoking blessings upon the Prophet is essential for drawing closer to God

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Greetings of peace mean the standard Muslim greeting and also being at peace with the Prophet, accepting his message, yielding to him, and submitting to the Divine Law.
rows.anchor: refers to the standard Muslim greeting, “Peace be upon you,” but it also indicates being at peace with the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic tradition says all creation prostrates to God and also extends greetings of peace to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: trees, stones, and all creation prostrate to God (see 16:40; 22:18; 55:6), so too do they extend greetings of peace

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that on a walk around Makkah, every rock and tree greeted the Prophet with peace.
rows.anchor: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said, “I went out with the Prophet through the environs of Makkah. Every rock and tree welcomed him

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: The question implies that there is no creator besides God who provides; provision from heaven alludes to rain and from earth to plants.
rows.anchor: The question means, “Is there a creator other than God who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?”

rows.speaker: IJ
rows.claim: The question can also mean: who will provide for you if God withholds His provision?
rows.anchor: Who is it that will provide for you if He withholds His provision?

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some commentators read aw as “and”: believers are guided, while disbelievers are in manifest error.
rows.anchor: interpret this verse to mean, “And surely we (the believers) are guided and you (the disbelievers) are in manifest error”

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: Others retain aw's disjunctive force: either group may be astray or guided, according to the wording.
rows.anchor: Others maintain that the verse means, “We are astray or guided and you are astray or guided”

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The slight ambiguity that disbelievers might perceive in the wording is understood by some as a gentle invitation to embrace faith.
rows.anchor: The slight ambiguity that disbelievers might see in this verse is then understood by some as a gentle invitation to embrace faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For manifest error, the commentary directs readers to the note on 36:24.
rows.anchor: For manifest error , see 36:24c

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Muslims and disbelievers are each responsible for their own religion and deeds, not the religion or deeds of the other.
rows.anchor: this verse recalls that the Muslims and the disbelievers bear no responsibility for the religion of the other

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also evokes the principle that no person bears another's burden.
rows.anchor: it evokes the general principle that none shall bear the burden of another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the opening sentence of verse 13, the commentary refers to the nearly identical wording in 31:29.
rows.anchor: Regarding the first sentence of v. 13, see commentary on the almost identical phrasing in 31:29

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The date-stone husk image reiterates God's absolute sovereignty by emphasizing the complete powerlessness of all beings invoked besides Him.
rows.anchor: That the deities called upon do not possess so much as the husk of a date stone reaffirms God’s absolute sovereignty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the Resurrection, the invoked deities disown the idolaters; 10:28 portrays them denying they were worshipped, as Satan also disavows the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: They then disown the idolatry of the disbelievers, as in 10:28, where it is reported that they will say

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When all mankind is gathered, those worshipped besides God become enemies of their worshippers and deny their worship.
rows.anchor: when mankind is gathered together, such will be enemies unto them and deniers of their worship

rows.speaker: Aj, Q, Z
rows.claim: No one can inform people as God informs them.
rows.anchor: no one can inform you in the manner that God informs you (Aj, Q, Z)

rows.speaker: Aj, Z, R
rows.claim: In context, the phrase may mean that only God tells the truth about idols, especially matters of the Unseen that reason cannot deduce.
rows.anchor: only God tells you the truth regarding this matter (Aj, Z), especially as it pertains to the Unseen and cannot be deduced through reasoning (R)

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: The phrase may also refer to God's informing people about the events of the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: can also refer to the events on the Day of Resurrection (IK, Ṭ)
